extracted.intended_audience: law professors, patent scholars, IP practitioners, USPTO examiners, judges, and policy makers interested in patentable subject matter doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of the doctrine limiting what subject matter is eligible for patent protection (e.g., abstract ideas, natural phenomena, laws of nature), including its functions, limits, and interactions with other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/public-goods justification for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter should be patentable only if a public goods problem exists—i.e., patent protection is needed to provide incentives for production of the public good; if no such problem exists, subject matter patentability should be denied and the patentability inquiry should end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Original wording) “If no public goods problem exists, either because of the nature of the subject matter, or because other factors exist that adequately incentive production of the public good, then subject matter patentability should be denied and the patentability inquiry should end.” Use economic analysis to justify inclusion/exclusion of categories of subject matter rather than relying on intuition or historical attributions of economic reasoning by courts. Consider whether claimed subject matter genuinely requires patent incentives to be produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and administrability of categorical exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusions from patentable subject matter must provide clear rules that can be applied without individualized examination to economize on administrative costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bright-line categorical exclusions (e.g., past exclusions for business methods, living things) can be administrable for a period but often become overinclusive or unworkable with technological change. Anti-pattern: relying on categorical field exclusions that quickly become outdated as technology evolves. Example concerns: living things exclusion became anomalous with genetic engineering; algorithm exclusion with the advent of computers; business method exclusion blurred by IT and the internet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability versus vagueness tradeoff (bright-line rules vs flexible standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright-line exclusions can be clear but unstable over time; flexible standards (e.g., ‘‘abstract ideas’’) are more durable but often too vague and uncertain to serve as efficient gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible standards may survive technological change but lack sufficient precision to economize on administrative costs; bright-line rules may be administrable short-term but fail as technology changes. Consider the need to balance durability with clarity when designing or applying subject-matter rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate functional role: threshold exclusion vs limitation on claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether subject matter doctrine should function as a threshold gatekeeper excluding categories from entry (front‑door exclusion) or as a tool to limit the permissible scope of claims (scalpel to sever overly-broad claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current doctrine often operates to limit claim scope (e.g., abstract ideas and natural phenomena are used to avoid unduly broad claims) rather than to exclude whole fields at the threshold. Practical implication: exclusions that mainly require careful claim-drafting do not economize on administrative costs because examiners must evaluate claim breadth in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing uniformity costs by defining field boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter boundaries can be used to limit the technological diversity of inventions governed by uniform patent rules, thereby reducing 'uniformity costs' — distortions caused by one-size-fits-all rights that are too strong or too weak in particular fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using field exclusions can make it easier to achieve optimal protection within a narrower range of innovations. Anti-patterns/risks: excluding new fields may delay or derail socially valuable innovations; excluding newcomers may produce political economy problems (rent-seeking). Policy analysis is required to determine which fields belong inside or outside patentable subject matter boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for political economy and stakeholder diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering subject matter boundaries, account for the political and distributional effects: narrowing eligibility may exclude stakeholders whose participation generates valuable countervailing pressures against narrow private interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A less diverse community of innovators may reduce opposition to interest-group lobbying, raising the risk of rent‑seeking. Thus, the desirability of exclusions must weigh both efficiency (uniformity costs) and political-economy consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-specific policy analysis before excluding entire fields
rubrics_metrics.description: If the goal is to exclude fields where less protection is optimal, decisionmakers should engage in explicit policy analysis to identify which fields should be excluded from patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current doctrine lacks the policy analysis necessary to make informed field exclusions. Anti-pattern: relying on vague crosscutting standards (e.g., 'abstract ideas') that do not map to particular fields. Where possible, assess innovation conditions across fields before excluding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction and redundancy with other patentability doctrines (prior art, novelty, nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether subject matter exclusions are redundant with or distinct from prior art/novelty/nonobviousness requirements; courts sometimes treat excluded subject matter as though it were prior art in evaluating patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some scholars argue that rigorous application of prior art doctrines could resolve certain cases now decided under §101. However, the Patent Act’s statutory categories of prior art (§102) do not plainly cover newly discovered products/phenomena of nature, so subject-matter doctrine may go beyond §102. Be cautious about conflating §101 exclusions with §102/§103 analyses; the cases show doctrinal commingling and debate about proper boundaries (e.g., Bergy critique of Flook conflation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of products of nature and natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to products of nature or phenomena of nature raise the question whether the inventor's contribution is more the product of nature than human ingenuity; courts sometimes treat such discoveries as part of the public 'storehouse of knowledge'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Funk Brothers (mixed culture of bacteria) — Court treated natural qualities as unpatentable and the inventor's combination as 'hardly more than an advance in the packaging,' relying in part on an obviousness-like analysis. Debate exists whether such matters should be handled via derivation/prior art (§102/§103) or §101 exclusions. Consider whether the asserted invention is primarily the handiwork of nature or the product of human invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of derivation/originality arguments (§102(f)/derivation) for nature‑derived inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentators propose using derivation/originality doctrines to bar patents on inventions derived from nature (treating nature-derived material as if not the inventor's own subject matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed approach: treat material derived from nature as prior art or unoriginal in assessing obviousness. Limits: little authority supports extending §102(f)/derivation theory to cover nature-derived inventions under current law; courts in major gene-patent cases relied on §101 rather than derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern for unduly broad claims and preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: A key concern in §101 jurisprudence is whether claims are so broad that they would preempt use of an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon — effectively granting a monopoly over the underlying principle rather than a particular application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Morse (invalidating an eighth claim because it would give control over future inventions), Benson, Bilski, Grams. Breadth and preemption risk indicate that a claim is improperly directed to the principle/algorithm itself rather than a patent-eligible application. Evaluate whether the claim would 'wholly pre-empt' future uses or applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth should be tested against enablement and disclosure (§112) as well as §101
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims appear overly broad, the statutory grounds of enablement and adequate disclosure (§112) may be the appropriate vehicle to invalidate them rather than treating breadth as a §101 ineligibility problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that if the problem with a claim is that it is too broad, statutory grounds such as failure of enablement under §112 should arguably be the basis for invalidity. Anti-pattern: resolving what are effectively enablement/disclosure problems solely through §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical administrative readiness and examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO's ability to apply subject-matter boundaries depends on its expertise and record of prior art in new fields; new categories of patentable subject matter pose administrative challenges for the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, the PTO initially lacked necessary expertise in areas like business methods, biotechnology, and software, complicating examination. Implication: weigh the PTO's practical capacity to examine new fields when considering whether to expand or restrict eligibility; exclusions that exclude newcomers may avoid immediate administrative burdens but risk stifling innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer tailored remedies over categorical exclusions where possible (use subject-matter limits to avoid unduly broad claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter doctrine can be used as a tool to deny or invalidate particular claims that threaten to impose costs that exceed their benefits even if it cannot serve efficiently as a categorical threshold exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While categorical exclusions may be ill-suited to the current doctrinal form, §101 limitations remain useful as a 'scalpel' to carve out unduly broad claims. Consider whether other doctrines fail and whether §101 should operate as a backstop. Recognize doctrinal redundancy is common and may be justified when the interest at stake is important.
